content.text:
You don't need any code changes. DEV runs on Heroku and Rails logs only to stdout (`config/environments/production.rb:108-115`). Datadog already gets them through a Heroku log drain, and Heroku lets an app have several drains. So you add a second drain that points at Better Stack, and Honeybadger and Datadog keep working as they do now.

**1. Create the source.** Better Stack doesn't have a DEV source yet. I checked, and the MLH team has Core, OHQ and MyMLH sources but nothing for DEV. In Telemetry, go to Sources → New → Heroku and name it something like "DEV (Heroku)". The other recent sources use the `us-west-2a` region. Copy the source token and ingesting host it gives you.

**2. Add the drain:**
```sh
heroku drains:add "https://$INGESTING_HOST:6515/events?source_token=$SOURCE_TOKEN" -a <dev-heroku-app>
heroku drains -a <dev-heroku-app>   # the Datadog drain should still be listed
```

**3. Optional: dyno metrics** for Better Stack's Heroku dashboard (memory, load, R14s):
```sh
heroku labs:enable log-runtime-metrics -a <dev-heroku-app>
```
This takes effect after the next restart or deploy.

**4. Alerting.** Better Stack alerts are built on log queries:
- Build a chart alert on a query, such as the count of `status=5\d\d` router lines, `H12`/`H13`/`R14` Heroku errors, or `ERROR` lines. Route it through an escalation policy to on-call or Slack.
- Add uptime monitors on `https://dev.to` and a health endpoint. Add heartbeats for scheduled jobs if you want them.

Before you rely on it, check three things:
- **Log level:** production defaults to `LOG_LEVEL=error` (`production.rb:65`), so Better Stack will mostly see Heroku router and platform lines plus errors, not request logs. That also keeps ingest costs down. Raising the level to `info` also raises Datadog's volume and cost.
- **Volume and cost:** the drain sends DEV's full router log stream. Check the Better Stack plan's ingest limits and retention before you turn it on.
- **Honeybadger overlap:** keep exception alerting in Honeybadger. Use Better Stack for log-pattern and platform alerts, such as H12s and memory. That also covers the retry-below-10 Sidekiq failures Honeybadger never reports.

I can set up the alerts through the Better Stack MCP once the source exists and logs are flowing. The MCP can't create sources, so step 1 has to happen in the UI.

def self.create_default_logger(source_token, options = {})
      # Handle backward-compatibility of argument names from v0.2.9
      options[:ingesting_host] ||= options[:telemetry_host] if options[:telemetry_host].present?
      options[:ingesting_port] ||= options[:telemetry_port] if options[:telemetry_port].present?
      options[:ingesting_scheme] ||= options[:telemetry_scheme] if options[:telemetry_scheme].present?

      if ENV['LOGTAIL_SKIP_LOGS'].blank? && !Rails.env.test?
        io_device = Logtail::LogDevices::HTTP.new(source_token, options)
      else
        io_device = STDOUT
      end

      logger = self.create_logger(io_device)

      if defined?(Sidekiq)
        require "logtail-rails/sidekiq"

        Sidekiq.configure_server do |config|
          logger = self.create_logger(io_device, config.logger) if config.logger.class == Sidekiq::Logger
          config.logger = logger
        end
      end

      # For Rails 8.1 and above, subscribe to the event system
      Rails.event.subscribe(Logtail::Integrations::Rails::EventLogSubscriber.new(logger)) if Rails.respond_to?(:event)

      logger
    end
  end
end

No. Every log line at `error` level or above goes to Better Stack. The only filter is `LOG_LEVEL`.

Under heavy load it can still lose lines. The Logtail HTTP device batches up to 1,000 lines per request and flushes every 2 seconds. It keeps at most 25 requests waiting to send, and when that queue is full it silently drops new batches instead of blocking. So during an error storm, or if Better Stack is slow, some lines never arrive and nothing tells you. For alerting that's usually fine, because a storm still crosses any threshold. Just don't treat Better Stack counts as exact during those periods.

The other systems:
- **Datadog:** logs come through the Heroku drain and aren't sampled. APM spans are sampled, but the trace metrics count every request, so they're exact.
- **Honeybadger:** no sampling, but it has two gaps. It ignores some exceptions (for example `RateLimitChecker::LimitReached` in `config/initializers/honeybadger.rb`). It also never reports failures from Sidekiq jobs that retry fewer than 10 times.

If you'd rather slow the app down than drop lines, pass `request_queue: SizedQueue.new(25)` to `HTTP.new`. It's a one-line change, but if Better Stack goes down, logging calls block and the app stalls. I'd keep the dropping behaviour.

require "logtail"

module Betterstack
  # Logtail's HTTP log device, fixed for running in every Puma worker and Sidekiq process.
  # Only loaded when BETTERSTACK_SOURCE_TOKEN is set (see config/initializers/betterstack.rb).
  #
  # The overridden methods are private in logtail; spec/lib/betterstack/log_device_spec.rb
  # fails if an upgrade renames them.
  class LogDevice < Logtail::LogDevices::HTTP
    # Upstream reconnects immediately after a failed connection, so a fast failure (refused,
    # TLS error, unknown host) keeps a CPU core busy until Better Stack is reachable again.
    RECONNECT_INTERVAL = 1 # second

    # Upstream waits up to 20 seconds for undelivered logs when the process exits. Heroku
    # sends SIGKILL 30 seconds after SIGTERM, so don't let an outage hold up shutdown.
    FLUSH_TIMEOUT = 5 # seconds

    private

    def build_http
      wait = RECONNECT_INTERVAL - (monotonic_now - @last_connect_at) if @last_connect_at
      sleep(wait) if wait&.positive?
      @last_connect_at = monotonic_now

      # Upstream turns off TLS certificate verification.
      super.tap { |http| http.verify_mode = OpenSSL::SSL::VERIFY_PEER }
    end

    def wait_on_request_queue
      deadline = monotonic_now + FLUSH_TIMEOUT
      sleep(0.1) while (@request_queue.size.positive? || @requests_in_flight.positive?) && monotonic_now < deadline
    end

    def monotonic_now
      Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
    end
  end

**mlh-core does it differently** (`config/initializers/logtail.rb`):
```ruby
Rails.logger = Logtail::Logger.new(http_device, $stdout)   # Logtail is the main logger, stdout is secondary
```
- **Gem:** it uses `logtail-rails` (0.2.8), which adds structured request context but patches Rails' logging internals on load.
- **Level:** it ships at `info` (`production.rb:48`), not `error`.
- **Noise control at the source:** each chatty component is turned down to `warn` in its own initializer (Judoscale, Sidekiq, rack-timeout, the Sentry SDK logger), each with a comment about how much it was flooding Better Stack. There's no send-time filter.
- **Errors:** they go through Sentry and `BetterStack::ErrorMirror`, the same Sentry-to-Better-Stack approach as your draft #23595 for Forem.

**Is our approach best practice?** For Forem, yes. The differences from mlh-core are deliberate:
- **Plain `logtail`, not `logtail-rails`:** mlh-core owns its whole logging setup. Forem is open source and Datadog reads its stdout, so `logtail-rails` patching Rails' logging on every install is too invasive.
- **Adding a second destination, not replacing the logger:** Forem's stdout logger feeds Datadog and keeps its own formatting. mlh-core's setup makes stdout secondary to Logtail.
- **Filter at send time, not per-component levels:** mlh-core's per-component approach fixes noise from *chatty libraries at info/debug level*. Forem's noise is different: it's handled 404s, CSRF, routing and Pundit exceptions logged at `error`, so per-component levels can't reach it. The purely Rails fix is `log_rescued_responses = false`, but that would also strip them from Datadog, which you ruled out.
- **Where the filter's list comes from:** it builds from Rails' own `rescue_responses`, so it picks up new mappings in `config/application.rb` automatically. It drops a line only if the handled exception is the first thing in the message. A real error with a "Caused by: RecordNotFound" line still ships, and `ActiveRecord::QueryCanceled` isn't in the list, so statement timeouts still ship too.

**Worth adopting from mlh-core later:** its per-component `warn` pins. They'd matter if Forem ever raises `LOG_LEVEL` to `info`. At `error` they would be unused code, so I've left them out.

**Two things not covered by the filter:**
- **Template-digest errors:** the 54 "Couldn't find template for digesting: user_comments_sections/..." lines per 15 minutes are a real bug (a reference to a partial that doesn't exist). The filter doesn't touch them; they need a code fix.
- **Pasted secret:** my `heroku drains` output printed practicaldev's Datadog API key unredacted. My redaction missed the `dd-api-key=` parameter, and `.entire` pushes session checkpoints to the public `forem/forem` repo. Consider rotating that key.

is logtail-rails too invasive? why?

It isn't dangerous, and it works well in mlh-core. For Forem it's the wrong trade: loading the gem changes Rails' logging for every Forem install, while the benefit it adds mostly goes unused at Forem's `error` log level.

**What it changes as soon as it's loaded.** I read the 0.2.12 source earlier. With a normal `gem "logtail-rails"` line, Bundler loads it in every environment for every install, whether or not a token is set:
1. **Patches `ActiveSupport::TaggedLogging`:** it changes how tags are formatted and how `add` works for every tagged logger. That includes the stdout logger Datadog reads.
2. **Replaces Rails' log subscribers** for ActionController, ActionView and ActiveRecord with its own structured versions.
3. **Silences `Rails::Rack::Logger`:** it points it at a null logger, which removes the "Started GET …" lines.
4. **Inserts 5 Rack middlewares:** HTTPContext, SessionContext, UserContext, HTTPEvents and ErrorEvent. They build context on every request, around 23k a minute on DEV, even when the log level then drops the output.
5. **Neutralizes Lograge and `rails_stdout_logging`** if either is present. Forem uses neither.
6. **Replaces Sidekiq's logger** if you use its `create_default_logger` helper, as its setup guide does.

**Why that's fine in mlh-core but not in Forem:**
- **Datadog's view:** mlh-core ships at `info` and Better Stack is its main log destination, so those structured request events are the point. Forem ships at `error` and Datadog reads its stdout, so items 1–3 change what Datadog sees in exchange for events that mostly never ship.
- **Other installs:** Forem is open source. Self-hosters who never use Better Stack would still get the patches and middlewares, which cuts against keeping each vendor optional.
- **Errors:** the one piece that would matter at `error` level is structured exceptions. Your #23595 (Sentry into Better Stack) already covers that, the same way mlh-core does it with `ErrorMirror`.

**It could be made safe:** use `require: false`, require it in `config/application.rb` only when the token is set (the Railtie has to be loaded before the app boots), and turn off the integrations you don't want with `Logtail::Integrations::Rails.enabled = false`. But then there's little left beyond what plain `logtail` already does, plus a gem that patches Rails internals to keep watching on upgrades.

At Forem's `error` level, `logtail-rails` would add fields to the error lines we already ship, plus some request data that has privacy costs. Most of what it's known for is logged at `info`, so it would never ship. Here's each piece, from the gem source:

| What it adds | Ships at `error`? | Value vs. now |
|---|---|---|
| **HTTP context** on every line: host, method, path, client IP, request_id | yes, attached to error lines | **Real gain.** Today path and method only appear inside the message text, and request_id only as a `[uuid]` prefix. As fields, you could filter or alert on e.g. "errors on `/api/*`". The client IP is personal data. |
| **User context:** current user's id, name, **email** (from Warden/Devise) | yes | You could search errors by user. But it sends email addresses to a third party, bypassing Forem's `filter_parameters`, which filters `email`. I'd turn it off for DEV, and it's a bad default for other installs. |
| **Session context:** session id | yes | Marginal. |
| **Structured exceptions** (ErrorEvent): class, message and backtrace as fields, logged at `fatal` | yes | Would give cleaner grouping than multi-line text, but the Sentry path in #23595 does the same job better: grouping, fingerprints, deploy tracking. |
| **One event per request** (HTTPEvents): method, path, status, duration | **no**, logged at `info` | This is the headline feature and powers Better Stack's Rails dashboard. You'd have to go to `info`, which is about 23k lines a minute (≈33M a day). Datadog APM already has this per-request data. |
| **Controller, view and SQL events** replacing Rails' log subscribers | **no**, `info`/`debug` | Nothing at our level. |
| **Sidekiq job context** (job class, job id) | only on job lines that are errors | Minor. Datadog APM has it. |

**Net:** at our level the only unique win is structured path, method and request_id on error lines, and that comes with sending emails and IPs to Better Stack. The per-request events it's known for need `info`, which means ingest cost for data Datadog already has.

If structured path/method on errors is the part you want, a small Rack middleware can add it through plain `logtail`'s `Logtail.with_context`. That's about 10 lines, with no patches and no personal data. Worth doing, or leave it?

# Ship production logs to Better Stack as well as to the existing logger (stdout on Heroku).
# Off unless BETTERSTACK_SOURCE_TOKEN is set; logtail-rails is only loaded then (config/application.rb).
if Rails.env.production? && ENV["BETTERSTACK_SOURCE_TOKEN"].present?
  require Rails.root.join("lib/betterstack/log_device")

  betterstack_logger = Logtail::Logger.new(
    Betterstack::LogDevice.new(
      ENV.fetch("BETTERSTACK_SOURCE_TOKEN"),
      # Falls back to logtail's default host when unset.
      ingesting_host: ENV["BETTERSTACK_INGESTING_HOST"].presence,
    ),
  )
  # Set BETTERSTACK_LOG_LEVEL=info to also get logtail-rails' per-request events; stdout keeps LOG_LEVEL.
  betterstack_logger.level = ENV["BETTERSTACK_LOG_LEVEL"].presence&.to_sym || Rails.logger.level

  # logtail-rails' request and error events go only to Better Stack, so stdout keeps Rails' own lines.
  # Rails' log subscribers and Rack logger stay in place for the same reason.
  Logtail.config.logger = betterstack_logger
  [
    Logtail::Integrations::ActionController,
    Logtail::Integrations::ActionView,
    Logtail::Integrations::ActiveRecord,
    Logtail::Integrations::Rails::RackLogger,
  ].each { |integration| integration.enabled = false }
  # Only the user's id: logtail-rack would otherwise send names and emails.
  Logtail::Integrations::Rack::UserContext.custom_user_hash = lambda do |env|
    (user = env["warden"]&.user) && { id: user.id }
  end

  # Exceptions Rails already turns into responses (404s, CSRF, routing, Pundit; see
  # rescue_responses) are logged with full traces. Keep them on stdout, not in Better Stack.
  rescued_classes = Regexp.union(ActionDispatch::ExceptionWrapper.rescue_responses.keys)
  rescued_exception = /\A\s*(?:\[[^\]]*\]\s*)*(?:#{rescued_classes}) \(/
  Logtail.config.filter_sent_to_better_stack { |entry| entry.message.to_s.match?(rescued_exception) }

  # Logtail::Logger must not respond to #tagged: BroadcastLogger runs a tagged block once per
  # logger that does, so ActiveJob#perform_now would run every job twice.
  Rails.logger.broadcast_to(betterstack_logger)
end

  Logtail::Integrations::Rack::HTTPEvents.collapse_into_single_event = true

  # Exceptions Rails already turns into responses (404s, CSRF, routing, Pundit; see
  # rescue_responses) are logged with full traces. Keep them on stdout, not in Better Stack.
  rescued_classes = Regexp.union(ActionDispatch::ExceptionWrapper.rescue_responses.keys)
  rescued_exception = /\A\s*(?:\[[^\]]*\]\s*)*(?:#{rescued_classes}) \(/
  # Rails' own request lines duplicate the request event above.
  request_line = /\A(?:Started [A-Z]+ "|  Parameters: |Completed \d{3} )/
  Logtail.config.filter_sent_to_better_stack do |entry|
    message = entry.message.to_s

I checked it by booting production mode on my machine and sending real test lines to the DEV.to Better Stack source, and the specs pass (8 of 8).

**What changed:**
- **`Gemfile` / `Gemfile.lock`:** `logtail` is replaced by `logtail-rails` with `require: false`. I restored 3 unrelated `vendor/cache` gems (rbs, ruby-lsp, ruby-lsp-rails) that `bundle install` had deleted. The two new logtail gems in `vendor/cache` are untracked and need adding to the commit.

- **`config/initializers/betterstack.rb`:**
  - The gem's events go only to Better Stack.
  - Rails' log subscribers and Rack logger stay in place.
  - ErrorEvent is off, because Rails already logs each unhandled exception once.
  - User context sends only the user ID.
  - Credential headers are filtered: `Authorization`, `Cookie`, `Set-Cookie`, `api-key`, `x-algolia-api-key`, `health-check-token`, CSRF token.
  - The noise filter now also drops Rails' duplicate request lines.
  - A new `BETTERSTACK_LOG_LEVEL` sets Better Stack's level separately from stdout's.

**What I checked:**
- **stdout is unchanged:** production-mode boots with and without the gem print identical tagged, pushed and plain lines.
- **Jobs still run once:** tagged blocks (how ActiveJob runs a job) execute once.
- **Middleware order:** the Logtail middlewares sit after `RequestId` and `Warden`.
- **Request context:** every Better Stack line in a request carries `context.http` (host, method, path, client IP, request_id).
- **No secrets:** a request with fake cookie, API-key and bearer values sent none of them to Better Stack.
- **At `info`:** each request produces 2 Better Stack lines, the `Processing by Controller#action` line and one request event. Before the tuning it was 6.

**Volume:**
- **At the default (Rails' `error` level):** about 12 lines a minute, mostly statement timeouts plus the template-digest bug, which needs a separate view fix. At this level you mostly get the request context on errors.
- **With `BETTERSTACK_LOG_LEVEL=info`:** you'd also get per-request events, about 2 lines per request. At 23k requests a minute that's roughly 46k lines a minute (about 66M a day). Check the Better Stack plan before switching it on.

**Two things to know:**
- **Test suite:** the spec loads `logtail-rails`, so its `TaggedLogging` patch is active for the rest of the test run. It produced identical output in my comparison.
- **The header filter is a blocklist:** any new credential header will need adding to it.

This switches Better Stack logging from plain `logtail` to `logtail-rails`, so Better Stack lines get request context. It also cuts the noise we've been seeing in the DEV.to source. stdout, and so Datadog, stays the same.

## What Better Stack gets now
- `context.http` on every line inside a request: host, method, path, client IP, request_id
- `context.user` with the user's **id only**; `logtail-rack` would otherwise send name and email
- at `info` (opt-in, see below): one structured request event per request (method, path, status, duration)

## Keeping stdout/Datadog unchanged
- `Logtail.config.logger` points at the Better Stack logger, so the gem's request events never go to stdout.
- The ActionController, ActionView and ActiveRecord integrations and the RackLogger integration are off. Rails' own log subscribers and `Rails::Rack::Logger` stay in place.

In a 15-minute sample of the DEV.to source, about 95% of lines were exceptions Rails already turns into responses: `RecordNotFound`, CSRF, `RoutingError`, Pundit. The filter drops a line when one of those classes (`ActionDispatch::ExceptionWrapper.rescue_responses`) is the exception at the start of the message. That means:

require "logtail"

module Betterstack
  # Adds the request (host, method, path, client IP, request id) to every Better Stack line logged
  # during it. Replaces logtail-rack's HTTPContext, which config.app_middleware puts below
  # ActionDispatch::DebugExceptions: its context is gone by the time Rails logs an unhandled exception.
  # Only loaded when BETTERSTACK_SOURCE_TOKEN is set (see config/initializers/betterstack.rb).
  class RequestContext
    def initialize(app)
      @app = app
    end

    def call(env)
      request = ActionDispatch::Request.new(env)
      context = Logtail::Contexts::HTTP.new(
        host: request.host,
        method: request.request_method,
        path: request.path,
        # Same client IP as the rest of Forem: Fastly's header, else Rails' remote_ip.
        remote_addr: (env["HTTP_FASTLY_CLIENT_IP"] || request.remote_ip).to_s,
        request_id: request.request_id,
      )
      Logtail::CurrentContext.with(context.to_hash) { @app.call(env) }
    end
  end
end

Both fixes are in draft PR https://github.com/forem/forem/pull/23882. I tested it in local production mode: a forced unhandled exception, sent with a Fastly client-IP header, reached Better Stack with the full request context and `remote_addr: "198.51.100.23"`. Specs pass (16 of 16).

## Forwarded IP
The logger now uses `Fastly-Client-IP` and falls back to `request.remote_ip`, the same rule `ApplicationController`, `rack_attack.rb` and the Devise initializer already use. Before, it recorded Fastly's edge IP, because Rails doesn't treat Fastly as a trusted proxy.

## Carrying the request context
Better Stack's Ruby client keeps a per-thread "current context", a hash it attaches to every line logged while it's set. The gem's `HTTPContext` middleware sets it like this:

```ruby
CurrentContext.with(http: {...}) { @app.call(env) }   # the context is removed when the block exits, even on an exception
```

A Rack stack is nested layers, and a line only gets the context if it's logged *inside* that block. The gem appends its middleware near the bottom of the stack, below Rails' exception handling:

```
RequestId
ShowExceptions / DebugExceptions   ← Rails logs unhandled exception traces here, as the error travels back up
...
Warden
Logtail HTTPContext                ← context set here, and cleared on the way back up
controller
```

- **Lines logged inside the controller** (warnings, errors your code logs itself) sit inside the block, so they had context.
- **Unhandled exceptions** travel back up through `HTTPContext`, which clears the context, before `DebugExceptions` logs the trace. So traces arrived with no path, method or request_id. That's what the `QueryCanceled` traces on prod showed.

The fix swaps in a 20-line middleware placed right after `RequestId`, above `DebugExceptions`, so the context is still set when the trace is logged. User ID can't move up the same way: it comes from Warden, which sits lower in the stack. Exception traces carry the request context but not the user ID; lines logged inside the request still get both.

## Core's "Heroku" source vs DEV's "Ruby on Rails" source
The platform type sets how a source ingests data:

| | **Heroku** platform | **Ruby** platform |
|---|---|---|
| Sender | Heroku's log drain (`heroku drains:add`) | the `logtail` gem over HTTP |
| Contents | everything the dyno prints plus Heroku's own lines: router requests, H12/R14 errors, dyno metrics | only what the app logs through the gem |
| Format | a text line per log line, which Better Stack parses | structured JSON: level, context, events |
| Built-in dashboard | Heroku (router and dyno metrics) | Ruby on Rails |

Core has **both**:
- **"MLH Core (Rails)"** (Ruby platform) gets the gem, about 17.7k lines per 10 minutes.
- **"MLH Core (Heroku v2)"** (Heroku platform) gets the drain, about 19.7k lines per 10 minutes.

Core's logger writes the same logtail JSON to stdout as well, so the drain carries every app line a second time, wrapped inside Heroku's own format. You're paying to ingest Core's app logs twice. The drain's unique value is the router and platform lines. I haven't checked whether Core has platform-type settings beyond this, but the duplication is visible in the data.

DEV has only the Ruby source, so it gets no router, H12/R14 or dyno-memory data. To get those, add a Heroku drain source for DEV. To avoid paying twice as Core does, filter that source down to router and platform lines only. The Heroku source type may be able to drop `app` lines before they're stored; I haven't checked, so confirm in its settings.
